questions.q: Why does the lesson call raw qubit count a 'marketing number, not an engineering one'?
options: Engineers never look at qubit count for any purpose, including setting an upper bound on problem size
Qubit count is always fabricated by vendors and never reflects a real physical device
Qubit count only matters for classical computers, never for quantum ones

A qubit that can't hold a useful state long enough or can't be reached by the qubits it needs to interact with contributes almost nothing to what the device can actually compute, so more low-quality qubits don't mean more real computing power
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that scaling up the count of noisy physical qubits without controlling their quality (fidelity) and their connectivity just adds more noise, not more usable computing power.

questions.q: Why can a device's average single-qubit gate fidelity look excellent while the device still struggles to run a real algorithm?
options: Because two-qubit gate fidelity and readout fidelity are usually noticeably worse than single-qubit fidelity, and a circuit that leans on two-qubit gates or depends on accurate measurement will feel those weaker numbers much more
Because single-qubit fidelity and two-qubit fidelity are always mathematically identical on real hardware
Because average fidelity numbers are never published by any vendor
Because fidelity has no relationship to whether a circuit produces a correct result
questions.explain: A device has several different fidelity numbers (single-qubit, two-qubit, readout) that matter differently; two-qubit gates are typically the limiting factor, so a circuit relying heavily on entangling gates is exposed to that weaker number.

questions.q: A circuit needs two qubits to interact that are not adjacent on a device's real topology. What happens, and why does it matter for fidelity?
options: The compiler inserts extra SWAP operations built from real two-qubit gates to move the information into position, and each inserted SWAP carries its own two-qubit error rate -- so a sparsely connected device can turn a clean circuit into a much deeper, noisier one
The device automatically rewires its physical connectivity graph at runtime with no fidelity cost
The circuit simply fails to compile and cannot run on any device
Connectivity has no effect on compiled circuit depth or error accumulation
questions.explain: SWAP networks route non-adjacent qubits into contact, but each SWAP is itself composed of two-qubit gates with real error rates, so poor connectivity can silently increase both circuit depth and total error even when qubit count and gate fidelity are unchanged.

questions.q: What does the lesson's 'three-way AND' rule say about qubit count, coherent circuit depth, and connectivity?
options: Only one of the three factors needs to be strong for a circuit to run successfully
Coherent circuit depth and connectivity are two names for the same underlying property

A circuit is only runnable if a device has enough qubits, enough coherent depth, and enough connectivity all at the same time -- being excellent on any two but weak on the third still makes a circuit unrunnable
Qubit count alone determines runnability, and the other two factors are secondary refinements
questions.explain: The three requirements are joined by 'and,' not 'or' -- for example, large qubit count with poor connectivity can burn the coherent-depth budget on SWAP overhead before the real algorithm runs, so excellence on two factors doesn't compensate for weakness on the third.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should you ask for in addition to qubit count before judging whether a device can run your real circuit?
options: The total number of research papers published about the device
Only the device's physical size and its manufacturer's name
Nothing else -- qubit count alone is sufficient to predict real-world performance
The two-qubit gate fidelity on the specific qubit pairs the circuit would use, and whether the device's connectivity graph already contains the connections the circuit needs
questions.explain: The lesson closes by naming the specific follow-up questions that actually predict runnability: two-qubit fidelity on the relevant qubit pairs, sustainable circuit depth, and whether the needed connections already exist in the topology.
